data.content_ref: inline:The target claims to 'avoid induction because it makes no claim about the future,' yet its own mechanism recommends choosing theory T 'to act on because it is the current least-worst known option, the one that has proven most resilient.' Acting on a theory is an inherently future-directed commitment: one selects T for action precisely because one expects T to remain adequate going forward. This expectation is an inductive inference from past resilience to future reliability—the very bridge the account disclaims. The claim thus self-undermines: it can preserve its anti-inductive posture only by refraining from any recommendation to act, but the mechanism explicitly does recommend action, smuggling in the induction it claims to dissolve. The countercondition ('If resilience in the past is logically irrelevant to resilience in the future without an inductive bridge') is therefore not merely an external risk but an internal contradiction: the account's own practical recommendation depends on the bridge it refuses to construct.
